name: Caro-Kann Defence
goal: As Black against 1.e4, you can play the Caro-Kann: support d5 with the c-pawn on c6, bring out the bishop on c8 early, and keep a solid position.
intro: The Caro-Kann answers 1.e4, White's pawn to e4, with 1...c6, your c-pawn one step forward, and then ...d5. The c-pawn backs up the d-pawn, so you keep a firm share of the centre. Unlike 1...e6, which shuts the bishop on c8 in behind a pawn, it leaves that bishop a clear road out as soon as the d-pawn has moved, and the bishop comes out early. You get a solid position with few weak points for White to attack.

parts.title: Bishop out before the pawns close
parts.keyIdea: Support your centre pawn with the c-pawn, and bring the light-squared bishop out before your e-pawn shuts it in.
parts.text: You are Black, and White opens with 1.e4. The moves you will play are known as the Classical Variation. At each move, ask what it does for your centre and your pieces, and what White is threatening.
parts.line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7

notes.text: 1...c6 looks modest, but it is there to support ...d5: if White ever takes a pawn on d5, your c-pawn can take back. Your e-pawn stays at home, so as soon as your d-pawn moves to d5, the bishop on c8, the one that moves on light squares, has an open diagonal and can come out early.
White has two pawns in the centre. 2...d5 challenges the pawn on e4 at once. If White takes with 3.exd5, you take back with the c-pawn and still have a pawn in the centre.
3.Nc3 guards e4. 3...dxe4 takes the pawn anyway: White's e-pawn is gone, and after the knight takes back, your next move can attack it.

4...Bf5 starts the Classical Variation, one of the named ways to play this opening. It develops the bishop, which means it brings it off its starting square, before ...e6 can shut it in, and it attacks the knight on e4. 4...Nd7 and 4...Nf6 are the other main moves.
5.Ng3 attacks your bishop. 5...Bg6 keeps it on the same diagonal, in front of your pawns, where it still aims at d3 and c2 in White's half of the board.
6.h4 threatens 7.h5, and then the bishop on g6 would have no good square left, because your own pawn on h7 blocks its way back. 6...h6 makes room: after h5, the bishop can drop back to h7.

7.Nf3 aims at e5, where a white knight would attack your bishop on g6. 7...Nd7 guards e5, so a knight that lands there can be taken. Next you play ...e6, bring your other knight from g8 to f6, bring out the bishop on f8, and castle.
